title: How do you optimize AWS costs: use Reserved Instances / Savings Plans for predictable workloads, Spot Instances for fault-tolerant batch jobs, right-size instances using CloudWatch metrics, use S3 lifecycle policies to move old data to cheaper storage tiers (S3-IA -> Glacier), turn off dev/test environments at night?
keyPoints: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances give up to roughly seventy percent off on-demand for steady, predictable workloads committed for one or three years.
Spot Instances use spare capacity at up to ninety percent off for fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work.
Right-sizing uses CloudWatch utilization metrics to match instance types to actual demand, eliminating waste.
S3 lifecycle policies move aging data to cheaper tiers automatically, saving over ninety percent on cold storage.
Shutting down dev/test environments nights and weekends cuts their cost by roughly two-thirds.
Cost optimization is a continuous discipline with tagging for attribution, budgets for alerts, and regular reviews.

s1_definition.oneliner: Cut AWS cost by committing to Savings Plans for steady workloads, Spot for interruptible batch, right-sizing from CloudWatch metrics, S3 lifecycle tiering for old data, and shutting off dev/test when idle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Savings Plans / Reserved Instances** – commit to one or three years of usage for large discounts (up to ~70% off on-demand) on steady workloads.
- **Spot Instances** – use spare AWS capacity at up to ~90% off for fault-tolerant, interruptible work; AWS can reclaim with two-minute warning.
- **Right-sizing** – match instance types to actual utilization using CloudWatch metrics and Compute Optimizer recommendations.
- **S3 lifecycle policies** – automatically transition aging data to cheaper storage tiers and expire old objects.
- **Environment scheduling** – shut down non-production environments outside working hours to eliminate idle spend.
- **Cost attribution** – tag all resources so each team sees its own spend; set budgets and alerts for surprises.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of running National Bank of India's branches. Savings Plans are like signing a long-term lease on the branches you always need, getting a big discount versus paying daily rates. Spot Instances are like cheap temporary staff for overflow work you can pause anytime. Right-sizing is noticing a branch has ten tellers but only needs four. S3 lifecycle tiers are moving old files from the expensive front office to a cheap basement. Turning off dev/test at night is switching off the lights in rooms nobody uses.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cost optimization on AWS is about matching supply to real demand and paying the lowest appropriate price for each workload without hurting performance or reliability. For steady, predictable workloads I commit to a Savings Plan for up to roughly seventy percent off on-demand. For fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work I use Spot Instances at up to ninety percent off. For everything running, I right-size continuously using CloudWatch metrics and Compute Optimizer. For storage, S3 lifecycle policies move aging data to cheaper tiers automatically.

Beyond compute and storage, I schedule dev/test environments to shut down nights and weekends (cutting their cost by about two-thirds), tag all resources for cost attribution so each team sees its own spend, and set budgets and alerts to catch surprises early. I also clean up waste like unattached EBS volumes and idle load balancers.

The senior point is that cost optimization is a continuous discipline, not a one-time cleanup, and it must never silently trade away reliability. I combine levers: commit to the steady baseline, burst above it on Spot or on-demand, and keep right-sizing as usage changes.

At National Bank of India I applied this mix. The always-on core ledger went onto a Savings Plan. The nightly fraud-analysis batch ran on Spot. I right-sized a fleet of web servers that CloudWatch showed running at ten percent CPU. Old statement data moved through S3 lifecycle tiers into Deep Archive. Dev/test environments switched off every evening and weekend. Together these cut our monthly bill substantially with no impact on production reliability.

Remember one sentence: optimize AWS costs with Savings Plans for steady workloads, Spot for batch, right-sizing from metrics, S3 lifecycle tiering, and environment scheduling -- it is a continuous discipline, not a one-time project.
